Issued at 128 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

All eyes are on the approaching vigorous upper low/trough located 
over southern Alberta/northern Montana early this afternoon. A sharp 
trough axis is rounding the southern periphery of this upper low, 
and the attendant upper jet max will arrive over eastern 
Montana/western North Dakota later this afternoon. At the surface, a 
sharp frontal boundary is sweeping eastward across Montana, and 
thunderstorm development has already ongoing along this frontal
boundary as of 18Z. Clearing of low stratus and patchy fog, 
along with limited coverage of high clouds, has allowed for 
destabilization of the atmosphere across much of North Dakota. 
As of 18Z SPC Mesoanalysis suggests 1500-2000 J/kg MLCAPE exists
across the northern and western portions of the state east of a
pseudo- dryline that is generally in the vicinity of the MT/ND 
stateline. Additionally, a warm front is draped from northwest 
to southeast across the state with backed easterly/southeasterly
low-level flow along it. As the cold front and accompanying 
line of showers and storms continues eastward, it will run into 
this unstable airmass and likely become severe (if it's not 
already). Generally speaking, the environment across the western
2/3rds of the state will support wind gusts up to 75 mph. In 
addition, with effective shear expected to be in the 
neighborhood of 30 knots, any storm that can become semi-
discrete may pose a large hail threat with up to golfball size 
hail possible. Lastly, backed low-level flow along the warm 
front will modestly enlarge low-level hodographs posing an 
isolated tornado threat as the line of storms sweeps across the 
state. One quirk in today's forecast is that a very tight 
pressure gradient will accompany this cold front. Therefore, it 
may be possible some locations see very little rainfall while 
experiencing a brief period of strong winds, especially across 
western North Dakota where the airmass is expected to be much 
drier than the rest of the state. 

The surface low and upper low are still forecast to become 
vertically stacked over Saskatchewan and will strengthen Monday 
morning. A resulting tight pressure gradient will reside along the 
international border and into much of North Dakota Monday morning 
into early Monday afternoon. The latest EFI, along with 
deterministic guidance, continues to trend upwards with the 
potential for strong wind gusts across far northern portions of the 
state. Ample diurnal heating should allow for a deeply mixed 
boundary layer, and uniform flow in said boundary layer should allow 
for strong winds aloft to be efficiently transferred to the surface. 
Guidance continues to show 850 mb winds in the 45 to 55-knot range. 
Assuming optimal conditions, 45 to 55 mph wind gusts appear likely 
across northern North Dakota during the day on Monday. A wind 
advisory has been hoisted for this potential across northern 
portions of the state. Late afternoon into early evening, the 
pressure gradient is forecast to relax, and wind speeds and gusts 
should gradually weaken through the evening and nighttime hours. In 
addition to the windy conditions, a much drier post-frontal airmass 
is expected to overspread much of the northern plains. Locations 
across western North Dakota could see minimum RH values around 20-
25% during the day on Monday. As a result of these dry and windy 
conditions, near-critical to critical fire weather conditions are 
appearing increasingly likely across western North Dakota. The main 
caveat to potential fire weather concerns is that recent rainfall 
will likely mitigate the volatility of fuels somewhat, 
therefore, a Red Flag Warning is not anticipated at this time.

Periodic chances for showers and storms remains in the forecast from 
Tuesday through the end of next week. Mid to long range guidance 
continues to be on board with a series of systems traversing the 
northern plains around mid/upper ridging remaining over the central 
and southern plains. The best chances for showers and storms next 
week will likely be Wednesday night into Thursday morning as a stout 
upper trough is forecast to eject into the northern plains. A brief 
break is possible heading into the weekend, with only low (under 
20%) chances returning by late Saturday into early Sunday. At this 
time, severe weather is not expected for during these periods.
